prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed from the photo: the vanity needs real work, but the billed name is wrong. photo_008 shows a narrow green bath whose vanity has painted, dated-but-serviceable door fronts, while its base is physically compromised — a dark open gap under the countertop overhang where the base/toe-kick trim has come away, and a rough, dark, deteriorated strip down the exposed side panel edge to the floor. That is damage, not a faded finish; the billed claim_text "worn or faded finish on intact vanity" asserts an intactness the photo contradicts. Terra's own supporting rationale ("dark deterioration along its exposed side edge") describes a damage condition, not the condition it was supporting.

What the 2a prose DID contain: both halves of the truth — the general wear ("The vanity looks worn") and the actual base anomaly ("possibly not fully finished at the bottom—the toe-kick/base area is open or misaligned"). What it did NOT contain: any damage/deterioration/water-stain wording; it framed the base as incomplete installation and headlined the vanity as "worn" and "dated." Because the real problem is present in 2a prose, pass_2a is not the answer — 2a saw it.

Downstream stays faithful until naming. 2b split the compound 2a sentence into atomic bullets and emitted BOTH "The vanity cabinet surfaces appear worn" (exact join, bullet_index 4, the billed one) and "The vanity toe-kick or base area appears open or misaligned" — no bullet is missing. 2c dropped neither; both survived. So the first stage with a choice it got wrong is 2d, whose entire job is choosing the catalog name. With candidate_count 8 it took resolution_path "lexical_shortcut" with shortcut_reason "support_phrase_hit" — a keyword latch on "worn" — and landed on vanity_worn_finish. The correct name was available and demonstrably reachable in this very run: the sibling bullet from the same 2a sentence on the same photo resolved to vanity_damaged_or_water_stained. 2d bound a true-but-weak observation to an item carrying a false qualifier ("intact vanity") about an object the same photo shows is not intact. This maps onto the ladder's own rung: resolved to the wrong catalog item -> 2d.

Confidence is medium, not high, for one honest reason: judged only on its own input string ("The vanity cabinet surfaces appear worn"), 2d's pick is defensible, and an alternative reading blames 2b for fragmenting one compound vanity-condition observation into pieces, stripping the not-intact qualifier from the piece that got billed. I rejected that because 2b's split is faithful atomization — its job, done correctly, with every bullet individually true — whereas 2d is the stage that actually assigns names and had the right one among its candidates. The post-Terra routing gap does not apply: the condition reached Terra, Terra supported it, and it was billed (disposition accepted_for_work, accepted true).

photo_002.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see a **full gut-or-major-refresh kitchen**, but also a workable footprint and plenty of upside.

**What stands out immediately:**
- **Very dated finishes:** raised-panel cabinets, laminate/parquet-style flooring, tile backsplash, soffit/upper cabinetry, old lighting, and the built-in wall oven/cooktop arrangement all read several decades old.
- **Worn cabinetry:** doors/drawers appear misaligned or damaged in places; the sink-base area especially looks tired and may have moisture wear. Plan on replacement rather than just cosmetic paint unless boxes prove sound.
- **Aging appliances/layout:** separate cooktop and wall oven, refrigerator sitting outside the main cabinet run, and limited clear counter space make the kitchen feel inefficient by current standards.
- **Potential water-risk area:** inspect closely under the sink, along the dishwasher/sink-side cabinets, and at the floor around the sink for soft spots, staining, rot, or subfloor damage.
- **Flooring condition:** heavily worn and likely needs removal. The floor should be checked once exposed, especially where there is visible discoloration/finish loss.
- **Lighting/electrical likely need updating:** pendant fixtures are dated, and there appear to be relatively few convenient task-lighting options. A renovation should account for recessed/task lighting, under-cabinet lighting, and updated outlets/GFCI protection.
- **Open shelving/window wall:** this is a visual liability now, but could become a feature—new window treatment, drywall/trim repair, or a redesigned sink/window zone could improve it substantially.

**Positive renovation signals:**
- The room has a reasonably efficient **U-/L-shaped work zone** with the sink, cooking area, and refrigerator fairly close together.
- There is meaningful cabinet volume and enough floor area for a compact dining table or potentially a more useful island/peninsula, depending on adjacent-room dimensions.
- The cabinet wall may allow a cleaner modern plan: full-height pantry storage, a standard range, relocated refrigerator, and longer uninterrupted counters.

**Likely scope:** At minimum, new flooring, cabinets or cabinet rehabilitation, countertops, sink/faucet, appliances, lighting, paint, and backsplash. A prudent buyer should budget for hidden plumbing, electrical, subfloor, and wall repairs until inspections/open-up confirm otherwise.

- **Very dated finishes:** raised-panel cabinets, laminate/parquet-style flooring, tile backsplash, soffit/upper cabinetry, old lighting, and the built-in wall oven/cooktop arrangement all read several decades old.
- **Worn cabinetry:** doors/drawers appear misaligned or damaged in places; the sink-base area especially looks tired and may have moisture wear. Plan on replacement rather than just cosmetic paint unless boxes prove sound.
- **Aging appliances/layout:** separate cooktop and wall oven, refrigerator sitting outside the main cabinet run, and limited clear counter space make the kitchen feel inefficient by current standards.
- **Potential water-risk area:** inspect closely under the sink, along the dishwasher/sink-side cabinets, and at the floor around the sink for soft spots, staining, rot, or subfloor damage.
- **Flooring condition:** heavily worn and likely needs removal. The floor should be checked once exposed, especially where there is visible discoloration/finish loss.
- **Lighting/electrical likely need updating:** pendant fixtures are dated, and there appear to be relatively few convenient task-lighting options. A renovation should account for recessed/task lighting, under-cabinet lighting, and updated outlets/GFCI protection.
- **Open shelving/window wall:** this is a visual liability now, but could become a feature—new window treatment, drywall/trim repair, or a redesigned sink/window zone could improve it substantially.

**Positive renovation signals:**
- The room has a reasonably efficient **U-/L-shaped work zone** with the sink, cooking area, and refrigerator fairly close together.
- There is meaningful cabinet volume and enough floor area for a compact dining table or potentially a more useful island/peninsula, depending on adjacent-room dimensions.

**Likely scope:** At minimum, new flooring, cabinets or cabinet rehabilitation, countertops, sink/faucet, appliances, lighting, paint, and backsplash. A prudent buyer should budget for hidden plumbing, electrical, subfloor, and wall repairs until inspections/open-up confirm otherwise.

There are no discrete stains, no fraying at the door transition or wall edges, and critically the doorway threshold -- the highest-traffic point in the room, where wear appears first -- is the same tone as the rest of the field. Terra's "mottled wear and darker discolored areas" is reading carpet nap as damage. The human v1.1 adjudication (claim absent, work none, hard_false_billed) holds.

Attribution is pass_2a because the unsupported material claim is already stated in the 2a prose: "Appears worn/older and likely a replacement candidate." 2a asserted wear as an observation, not as a modernization/dated-ness judgment. Everything downstream carried that assertion faithfully and added no false meaning: 2b produced "The carpet appears worn and older." (exact join, bullet_index 2), 2c kept it among the five survivors, 2d resolved it to worn_or_stained_carpet via exact_kind lexical shortcut on a support-phrase hit, 2e kept it (kept_issue_ids includes 5f9c12d2fa0550e1), it projected to oc1_874eea526d4e2aab, and Terra supported it. The "or stained" wording is catalog family naming, not a distortion introduced at 2d -- the falsehood is the wear claim, and it is 2a's. What the 2a prose did NOT contain is any staining, fraying, or traffic-wear detail; it explicitly said "No obvious water staining, major cracking, or visible structural concerns" and called the room "a straightforward cosmetic renovation," so 2a had the correct read of the room available and still asserted carpet wear, apparently conflating dated/builder-grade with worn. 2a is therefore the first stage that went wrong.

photo_032.jpg.p2a_prose:
What jumps out to a renovator:

- **Very tight layout:** The toilet-to-vanity clearance is minimal, and the vanity door projects into the walking area. Reconfiguring to a smaller vanity, pedestal sink, or wall-hung sink could improve usability.
- **Vanity is at end of life:** Doors are misaligned/open, interior appears unfinished or missing shelving, and the cabinet/sink combo looks dated. Likely a straightforward replacement.
- **Visible wall repairs/unfinished work:** There are patch marks and scuffs around the vanity, plus what appears to be an unused/moved fixture location. Expect drywall repair, skim coating, and repainting.
- **Questionable electrical finish:** Outlet/switch plates and placements look inconsistent; verify GFCI protection, grounding, and whether any electrical work was done properly.
- **Possible plumbing/condition check needed:** The vanity base and floor area should be checked for water staining, soft subfloor, leaks, and mold—especially given the cabinet condition.
- **Flooring/transition looks recent or piecemeal:** Vinyl plank flooring is serviceable, but the doorway transition and perimeter finishing look rough. Confirm it is properly installed and not concealing floor damage.
- **Dated fixtures and storage:** Basic toilet, faucet, medicine cabinet, lighting, and trim would all likely be part of a cosmetic refresh.
- **Wall/trim quality:** Baseboards, caulking, and paint lines look incomplete or rough, suggesting this bathroom may have been partially updated without a full finish-out.

Overall, it reads as a **small, inexpensive cosmetic renovation with a need for careful plumbing/subfloor inspection**. The layout—not the finishes—is the main long-term limitation.

- **Strong original rowhouse character:** The red-brick façade, arched window heads, brownstone/stone base, projecting window sills, and ornate cornice/brackets are valuable period details worth preserving.
- **Good curb-appeal upside:** The basic façade reads more intact and cohesive than many heavily altered rowhomes. A restrained restoration—cleaning/repointing brick, repainting trim, upgraded door/lighting—could have a major payoff.
- **Brick and masonry need close inspection:** There appear to be areas of aging/discoloration and possibly prior patching. Check mortar condition, lintels/arches, settlement cracks, moisture entry, and whether any brick has been painted or improperly repointed.
- **Cornice/roofline is a key risk item:** The decorative metal/wood cornice looks largely present, but these can hide rot, corrosion, loose elements, and roof-edge drainage problems. Inspect from the roof rather than judging from this view alone.
- **Mixed/older windows:** Some windows look like older replacement units or varying styles. They may be serviceable, but a renovation should consider energy performance, air sealing, and retaining/restoring the historically prominent openings where feasible.
- **Basement-level opportunity and concern:** The visible lower-level windows suggest usable basement space, but also raise questions about waterproofing, ceiling height, egress, foundation condition, and whether it can legally be finished or rented.
- **Entry needs modernization:** The red door is a visual focal point but the stoop, railings, landing, house-number/mailbox setup, and exterior light could be upgraded for a cleaner, higher-end first impression.
- **Street tree is both asset and maintenance issue:** It softens the frontage but obscures the house and may contribute leaves/gutter clogging or root-related sidewalk issues. Pruning and checking sidewalk/root conditions would be sensible.
- **Tight attached-house renovation realities:** Any structural, plumbing, electrical, roof, or drainage work needs coordination with adjoining properties and careful party-wall assessment.

From this exterior alone, it looks more like a **character-preserving renovation with targeted envelope and systems work** than a façade needing wholesale rebuilding. The biggest unknowns are roof/cornice condition, rear façade condition, water intrusion, basement condition, and interior mechanicals.

photo_008.jpg.p2a_prose:
What stands out to a renovator:

- **Brick façade needs masonry review:** mortar joints look weathered/uneven in places, especially around the opening and lower wall. Budget for selective repointing and checking for spalling or moisture entry.
- **Front door/trim is tired:** the door has chipped paint, mismatched/aged hardware, and the white jamb casing shows peeling paint, open joints, and likely rot or deterioration at the bottom.
- **Transom is effectively blocked off:** the upper opening has been filled with horizontal panels rather than functioning glazing. Restoring it with an insulated transom window could improve light and curb appeal, but flashing and lintel conditions should be checked.
- **Entry waterproofing details deserve attention:** the threshold, sill area, and jamb-to-brick transitions are common leak points; they look like a likely maintenance item.
- **Concrete stoop/landing is serviceable but worn:** staining, rough patches, and edge wear suggest resurfacing or repair may be needed. Check slope/drainage so water is directed away from the door.
- **Lower masonry/base treatment is mismatched:** the darker foundation/parged area contrasts with the brick and appears patched. It may simply be cosmetic, but should be inspected for moisture, cracking, and loose material.
- **Quick curb-appeal upside:** a new/rehabbed door, restored trim/transom, cohesive house numbers/mailbox, refreshed railing, and masonry cleanup could materially improve the entrance without changing the façade.

Nothing in this single photo proves a major structural issue, but a renovator should prioritize a close inspection of the **lintel, brick mortar, door-frame rot, and water management at the stoop**.

prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed on my own reading of both photos. Photo_008 (entry close-up) shows a mismatched patched vertical strip of brick along the left door jamb with smeared, off-tone mortar, whitish staining/efflorescence on the brick faces, and a darker parged base treatment contrasting with the brick above; photo_001 (street view of #3227) shows tonal mottling across the brick field, soiling under the projecting sills and cornice, and a whitish repainted band at the first-floor base. Weathering/discoloration is modest but real, matching the adjudicated v1.1 axes (claim exact, work warranted) and the billed claim text "brickwork weathering or discoloration with intact mortar".

The 2a prose did NOT omit this. Photo_001's prose contains the condition explicitly ("Brick and masonry need close inspection: There appear to be areas of aging/discoloration and possibly prior patching"), and photo_008's prose contains it twice over ("mortar joints look weathered/uneven in places" and "the darker foundation/parged area contrasts with the brick and appears patched"). What the prose did NOT contain is any hedge that would license a later stage to distort it — no claim of a uniform facade, no assertion the brick was sound. So pass_2a is ruled out: the condition survives in both readings.

Walking the rest of the ladder, no earlier rung fails. 2b produced matching bullets on both photos ("Brick masonry shows aging and discoloration." idx 5; "The lower masonry base treatment is darker than the brick and appears patched." idx 6), both joined by exact method. 2c kept both — they appear in p2c_surviving, not p2c_dropped. 2d resolved both to brick_weathered_or_discolored via exact_kind routing, and that is the same item the human graded "exact", so the resolution is not wrong. 2e kept both issues (both issue_ids are in kept_issue_ids), and per the corpus rule 2e is not an available attribution regardless. Condition projection succeeded: both issues carry projected_condition_id oc1_261de865e0dd299d, so the condition existed and reached Terra.

Terra is therefore the first stage that went wrong. It returned verdict "unsupported" with the rationale "The visible brick facade appears generally uniform, with mortar joints intact and no clear weathering or discoloration," which drove disposition "excluded" and reason_code "verdict_unsupported". That rationale contradicts what the photos show, and it also misuses the claim's own wording: "with intact mortar" is part of the catalog claim's definition, not a fact that argues against it, so Terra cited a satisfied condition as grounds for rejection. This is not the post-Terra routing gap — Terra did not support the condition and then lose it downstream; Terra affirmatively rejected it, which is a rung the ladder covers.

photo_028.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see a good “bones and light” room with a fairly clear cosmetic scope:

- **Strong natural light:** Multiple large windows on two walls are a major asset. The room could feel dramatically better with cleaned-up trim and updated window treatments.
- **Original wood flooring:** It appears heavily worn, scratched, and stained, but it may be solid hardwood that can be refinished rather than replaced. Confirm thickness/condition and check for pet staining or moisture damage before assuming it will sand out.
- **Dated, rough window trim:** The wide painted trim has visible wear, uneven paint, gaps, and minor damage—especially at the lower left window. It could be restored for character or replaced for a cleaner, more contemporary look.
- **Wall/paint condition:** Walls show scuffs, small cracks/patches, and an aged finish. Prep, repairs, and fresh paint would make an immediate difference.
- **Baseboards and transitions:** Baseboards look tired and inconsistent, with possible gaps and rough paint; likely a repair/replace-and-repaint item.
- **Ceiling/crown molding potential:** The high-ish ceiling and simple crown molding are positives, though the molding/paint lines need cleanup. Updating the basic flush-mount light would help.
- **Electrical details:** Outlets and plates look dated, and there appears to be an older floor/wall vent arrangement. A renovator would verify grounding, panel capacity, and whether wiring is modernized.

Nothing in this photo alone proves a major structural issue, but the floor staining and damaged trim merit a closer moisture/window-leak inspection.

photo_003.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely notice:

- **Original character is intact:** Tall paneled doors, substantial painted trim, wide baseboards, and crown molding are worth preserving/restoring rather than replacing.
- **Potential hardwood floors:** The dark wood flooring appears original or older and heavily worn/paint-splattered. It may refinish well, but needs testing for thickness, stains, and repairability.
- **Cosmetic-heavy condition:** Scuffed doors, tired paint, stained floor finish, and dated vent cover suggest a straightforward visual refresh could make a major difference.
- **Plaster/wall movement to assess:** There are visible cracks and unevenness on the left wall. Could be minor settling/plaster deterioration, but a renovator would check for moisture, active movement, and loose plaster before finishing.
- **Dated mechanical/electrical details:** The low wall grille and older-looking outlet/cover warrant inspection of HVAC, wiring, and insulation—not just replacement of visible components.
- **Layout/door swing considerations:** Multiple doors clustered in a small area can affect furniture placement and circulation. The openings may offer an opportunity to improve flow, depending on what rooms they connect to and whether walls are structural.
- **Good ceiling height and proportions:** The room’s height and trim scale create strong renovation upside; cleaned-up walls, restored woodwork, updated lighting, and refinished floors could transform it without changing the footprint.

The main appeal is **restoration potential**, while the key due-diligence items are the wall cracking, floor condition, and age/condition of the systems behind the finishes.

- **Windows are inconsistent/aging:** The windows appear to be older replacements and may not match in style or finish. Inspect operation, seals, rot around trim, and energy performance; a coordinated window plan could improve appearance.
- **Basement windows:** Low basement openings need careful review for drainage, window-well protection if applicable, security, and potential egress requirements if the basement is finished or intended for living space.

- **Exterior detailing opportunity:** The building has good proportions, but the white-painted trim against the stone looks unfinished in spots. Cleaner trim detailing, repaired lintel/sill areas, and landscaping/pruning would make the façade feel much more intentional.

What the 2a prose did NOT contain is the specific vocabulary of the catalog item ("soffit," "porch ceiling panels," "loose or missing panels") -- it described the same physical defect at the porch-roof connection in roof/framing language rather than soffit language. That wording gap did not cost anything downstream: 2b lifted the sentence verbatim as bullet index 1 (exact join), 2c kept it (p2c_present true, and the only 2c drops on this photo are four benign non-defect bullets: low house, flat yard, large porch, mature trees), 2d resolved it via the llm path to soffit_or_porch_ceiling_failed on exact_kind routing -- a resolution the human's "exact" claim axis explicitly ratifies, so 2d is not the fault -- 2e kept the issue (p2e_status kept, issue id present in kept_issue_ids), and condition_projection produced oc1_69263601050587ce.

photo_005.jpg.p2a_prose:
To a renovator, this reads as a **functional but dated kitchen with a fairly contained cosmetic-refresh opportunity**.

**What stands out:**

- **Original/older layout and finishes:** Raised-panel white cabinets, laminate counters, small mosaic backsplash, vinyl sheet flooring, fluorescent-style range hood, and electric coil range all date the room.
- **Cabinets appear reusable:** They look generally intact and reasonably aligned. A budget renovation could include repainting/refacing, new pulls, soft-close hardware, and possibly replacing a few worn doors rather than a full cabinet tear-out.
- **Countertops are a major visual weakness:** The dark speckled laminate looks serviceable but dated and has limited backsplash integration. Replacing counters and adding a full-height tile backsplash would make a substantial difference.
- **Awkward corner storage:** The open curved corner shelving near the range is inefficient and visually busy. A renovator may consider a proper corner cabinet solution, pantry pull-outs, or a redesigned base-cabinet run.
- **Appliance package needs updating:** The white coil-top stove and older microwave are likely candidates for replacement. The kitchen would benefit visually from coordinated stainless or black appliances—assuming electrical/venting allows.
- **Range hood/venting is a key due-diligence item:** It appears to be a basic recirculating hood. Confirm whether it vents outdoors; adding exterior venting can be a meaningful upgrade and cost variable.
- **Flooring is ripe for replacement:** The vinyl is worn-looking and visually dated. LVP, tile, or a continuous floor into adjoining spaces would modernize it quickly.
- **Limited prep space:** The sink-side counter is crowded, and the dining table consumes much of the room. A layout rethink—smaller table, peninsula, or better storage—could improve usability if dimensions permit.
- **Window treatment and wall color are easy wins:** The floral valance/blinds and beige walls are purely cosmetic and inexpensive to modernize.
- **Potential concern to inspect:** The lower cabinetry/base areas, around the sink, and the floor near appliances should be checked for water damage, swelling, soft spots, or hidden leaks. Nothing severe is obvious in the photo, but these are typical risk zones.

**Bottom line:** This does not immediately look like a full gut-job from the photo. It looks like a strong candidate for a **mid-level kitchen refresh**—flooring, counters, backsplash, lighting, appliances, paint, hardware, and selective cabinet work—with a full remodel only if the owner wants to improve layout, storage, and ventilation.

With 7 candidates it took resolution_path=lexical_shortcut on shortcut_reason=support_phrase_hit -- i.e. it latched onto the token "worn" -- and resolved to the degradation item vinyl_linoleum_worn_or_stained, whose claim text asserts "vinyl or linoleum flooring staining, discoloration, or wear on intact material." The same photo's other dated-finish bullets resolved correctly to modernization items (outdated_kitchen_finishes, appliances_dated_or_basic), which is where a dated-flooring observation belonged. Terra therefore is not the first wrong stage; it verified correctly the claim it was handed. One caveat: the record exposes catalog kind only alongside the 2d-resolved item, so if the degradation kind label were assigned upstream at 2c rather than chosen at 2d, blame would shift one rung earlier; the recorded p2d shortcut mechanism is the concrete documented cause, so 2d is the call.

That matches the claim text "tub surround or shower pan cracked, chipped, or damaged wet-area enclosure" and matches the v1.1 adjudication (claim=exact, work=warranted). The condition was projected (oc1_c00cb1e0f1fdb9da) and then unbilled with disposition=excluded / reason_code=verdict_unsupported, so it is a miss.

Walking the ladder: 2a DID contain the condition — the prose names the enclosure twice ("a questionable curb/pan condition", "a new properly waterproofed pan and surround") and separately notes "the shower valve/trim appears incomplete or damaged". What the prose did not contain was the literal words "cracked" or "chipped"; it hedged the enclosure as "questionable" and "heavily compromised", but the condition is unmistakably present, so 2a is not the failure. 2b emitted the matching bullet and joined it exactly (bullet_index 4, method exact). 2c kept it (p2c_present true); it dropped the sibling bullet "The shower curb and pan condition is questionable.", but that drop cost nothing because the surviving bullet carried the same condition forward. 2d resolved to tub_surround_or_shower_pan_damage — the bullet is phrased about valve/trim while the item is about the enclosure, which is the one arguable hop, but the human adjudicated the resulting claim as EXACT, so by the truth basis 2d resolved correctly and is not the first wrong stage. 2e kept the issue, and per the record 2e never cost a condition here. condition_projection produced the condition and it reached Terra.

Terra is therefore the first stage that went wrong: it returned "unsupported" with the rationale that only staining was visible and "no clear crack, chip, or enclosure damage is visible", which the photo contradicts — the surround is physically broken open at two wall penetrations and the pan/curb is chipped and degraded. Terra's rejection is what caused the unbilling (reason_code verdict_unsupported), so this is a Terra verdict error, not the known post-Terra routing/disposition gap (that gap applies only when Terra supported the condition).

photo_022.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely notice:

- **A dated, chopped-up layout:** The central partition/soffit creates a narrow, awkward circulation area. It may be an opportunity to open the space up, subject to confirming whether any portion is structural or contains utilities.
- **Possible former kitchen/service area:** The tiled wall with decorative backsplash at right strongly suggests this adjoins or once contained kitchen cabinetry. The room may lend itself to a kitchen reconfiguration or a more open kitchen/living plan.
- **Exposed ceiling beam/bulkhead:** The long dropped element across the ceiling could be structural or could conceal mechanical/electrical runs—important to inspect before planning an open concept.
- **Mixed finishes and clear cosmetic updating needs:** Large-format beige tile, heavy dark wood trim, painted-over/dated doors, mismatched baseboards, and basic light fixtures all read as ready for modernization.
- **Potential flooring decision:** Tile is durable but visually dominates the room; replacing it—or continuing a more consistent flooring material into the adjoining rooms—could substantially improve cohesion.
- **Good opening sizes between rooms:** The broad cased opening on the right and adjacent rooms indicate potential for better sightlines and flow, even if full wall removal is not feasible.
- **Signs to investigate, not necessarily red flags:** Scuffs, uneven-looking trim/patching, and the prominent fire extinguisher warrant checking condition, property use/history, electrical, and whether permits/code requirements apply.

What 2a did NOT contain is any statement that the trim is thin or builder-grade — it consistently describes substantial, heavy, wide, original trim.

photo_015.jpg.p2a_prose:
To a renovator, this reads as a **functional but dated kitchen with a clear cosmetic-to-moderate renovation opportunity**.

- **Original/aged cabinetry:** Oak cabinets look worn and somewhat mismatched in layout; several doors are open, which may signal missing hardware, loose hinges, or simply poor presentation. Cabinet replacement—or at least repainting/refacing—would make the biggest visual difference.
- **Limited, awkward storage layout:** The upper cabinets stop and restart around the range, with a narrow open cubby. A redesign could improve storage and create a more intentional range/hood wall.
- **Dated laminate countertops and basic sink:** Counters appear serviceable but inexpensive and worn. Replacing counters, sink, faucet, and backsplash would modernize the room quickly.
- **Older white appliances:** The gas range and refrigerator look dated and mismatched. Budget for replacement and confirm gas connection, venting, and electrical capacity.
- **No visible backsplash:** There is an easy value-add opportunity for tile or a durable slab backsplash after countertop work.
- **Lighting is minimal:** A single flush-mount ceiling fixture is likely inadequate for a kitchen. Recessed lights, a brighter central fixture, and under-cabinet lighting would help considerably.
- **Flooring transition/condition:** The dark plank flooring in the kitchen contrasts with the carpeted adjacent area. It appears newer than the cabinetry but should be checked for moisture damage, soft spots, and installation quality—especially near the sink and refrigerator.
- **Potential layout opportunity:** The kitchen appears narrow but open toward an adjacent hall/living area. Depending on what is behind the walls, a renovator may look at widening the opening, adding a peninsula, or improving the visual connection to the next room.
- **Walls/ceilings:** Paint is dated but the surfaces do not show obvious major cracking in this photo. Still inspect for water staining, ventilation issues, and wall damage behind cabinets/appliances.

Overall: it looks like a **good candidate for a mid-level kitchen refresh**, with the main unknowns being plumbing, electrical, flooring condition, and whether the existing layout can be opened up without structural work.

So pass_2a is not responsible.

Every downstream rung before Terra also worked: 2b emitted a matching bullet on each photo (all three joins exact, indices 13/9/3), 2c kept all three survivors, 2d resolved all three to paint_refresh_recommended via exact_kind, and the issues projected to a single condition oc1_6ea2a14d497dece9 that reached Terra. Its rationale — "The visible wall colors are neutral and not clearly highly personalized or dated" — answers only the "highly personalized" half of the claim text and treats neutral hue as disqualifying, ignoring the dated beige/taupe/black-brick combination and the worn, patched paint condition that 2a, 2b, 2c and 2d all carried forward accurately. prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise holds on my own inspection. Photo_044 shows a dark-stained oak floor that, despite a glossy sheen, carries a distinct dark scuff/smear blemish in the center foreground plus fine surface scratching visible in the raking light across the left half; photo_048 shows the same flooring with clear board-to-board color variation and a dulled, worn finish along the traffic path toward the closet. That is exactly the catalog claim "hard flooring finish scratches, scuffs, or worn finish on intact flooring," and it matches the adjudicated v1.1 axes (claim=exact, work=warranted).

The 2a prose did NOT omit this. Both photos' prose name it in the first bullet: photo_044 says the hardwood floors "appear scuffed/worn in places and could benefit from refinishing or at least a deep clean and recoat," and photo_048 says they "could benefit from refinishing or at least a deep clean/polish; there may be minor wear and color variation." What 2a did not contain was any competing or hedged reading that would have weakened the condition -- it is stated plainly as wear needing refinishing, so pass_2a is not the failure.

Every intermediate rung also passed it through cleanly, so none of them can be first: 2b produced verbatim bullets ("Solid hardwood floors are scuffed and worn." and "Hardwood floors show minor wear and color variation.") and both joined with method=exact; 2c kept both as survivors rather than dropping them (2c's drops on these photos were unrelated -- registers, trim, natural light, closet doors); 2d resolved both to the correct catalog item hard_flooring_scratched_or_worn via routing_reason exact_kind, so there is no wrong-item error; 2e status is "kept" for both issues; and condition_projection succeeded, yielding condition oc1_523e4aed4e443052.

The condition therefore reached Terra fully formed, and Terra is where it died: terra_verdict "unsupported" with the rationale that the flooring "appears generally intact without clear scratches, scuffs, or worn finish," producing accepted=false and reason_code verdict_unsupported. That directly contradicts what the photos show. This is not the known post-Terra routing/disposition gap -- Terra did not support the condition and then lose it downstream; Terra itself rejected it -- so "unclear" does not apply. Terra is the first and only stage that went wrong.

- **Good bones / usable layout:** Rectangular room, decent ceiling height, closet storage, and an HVAC supply vent. The closet is already fairly modern with bypass paneled doors.

- **Wall condition:** Beige paint is dated and there are minor scuffs, dents, and possible patch marks. Expect prep work (patching, sanding, repainting), but no obvious major moisture damage in this image.
- **Trim/door mismatch:** Bright white baseboards and closet doors contrast with an older, plain interior door and basic hardware. A renovator may replace or repaint the bedroom door, update knobs, and standardize trim/finish.
- **Transom above the door:** The small interior transom is a distinctive older feature. It could be retained for character/light flow, restored, or enclosed if privacy/sound control matters.
- **Ceiling fan/light:** Dated and likely an easy replacement. Check ceiling box support if installing a heavier fan or modern fixture.
- **Heating/ventilation note:** The visible wall/floor register area and high wall vent should be checked for airflow and condition before boxing in or changing closet/wall configurations.
- **Possible wall-planning opportunity:** The large uninterrupted wall could accommodate built-ins, a larger wardrobe system, or a feature wall—but verify which walls contain mechanicals before altering anything.

photo_002.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see a **full gut-or-major-refresh kitchen**, but also a workable footprint and plenty of upside.

**What stands out immediately:**
- **Very dated finishes:** raised-panel cabinets, laminate/parquet-style flooring, tile backsplash, soffit/upper cabinetry, old lighting, and the built-in wall oven/cooktop arrangement all read several decades old.
- **Worn cabinetry:** doors/drawers appear misaligned or damaged in places; the sink-base area especially looks tired and may have moisture wear. Plan on replacement rather than just cosmetic paint unless boxes prove sound.
- **Aging appliances/layout:** separate cooktop and wall oven, refrigerator sitting outside the main cabinet run, and limited clear counter space make the kitchen feel inefficient by current standards.
- **Potential water-risk area:** inspect closely under the sink, along the dishwasher/sink-side cabinets, and at the floor around the sink for soft spots, staining, rot, or subfloor damage.
- **Flooring condition:** heavily worn and likely needs removal. The floor should be checked once exposed, especially where there is visible discoloration/finish loss.
- **Lighting/electrical likely need updating:** pendant fixtures are dated, and there appear to be relatively few convenient task-lighting options. A renovation should account for recessed/task lighting, under-cabinet lighting, and updated outlets/GFCI protection.
- **Open shelving/window wall:** this is a visual liability now, but could become a feature—new window treatment, drywall/trim repair, or a redesigned sink/window zone could improve it substantially.

**Positive renovation signals:**
- The room has a reasonably efficient **U-/L-shaped work zone** with the sink, cooking area, and refrigerator fairly close together.
- There is meaningful cabinet volume and enough floor area for a compact dining table or potentially a more useful island/peninsula, depending on adjacent-room dimensions.
- The cabinet wall may allow a cleaner modern plan: full-height pantry storage, a standard range, relocated refrigerator, and longer uninterrupted counters.

**Likely scope:** At minimum, new flooring, cabinets or cabinet rehabilitation, countertops, sink/faucet, appliances, lighting, paint, and backsplash. A prudent buyer should budget for hidden plumbing, electrical, subfloor, and wall repairs until inspections/open-up confirm otherwise.

photo_002.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see a **full gut-or-major-refresh kitchen**, but also a workable footprint and plenty of upside.

**What stands out immediately:**
- **Very dated finishes:** raised-panel cabinets, laminate/parquet-style flooring, tile backsplash, soffit/upper cabinetry, old lighting, and the built-in wall oven/cooktop arrangement all read several decades old.
- **Worn cabinetry:** doors/drawers appear misaligned or damaged in places; the sink-base area especially looks tired and may have moisture wear. Plan on replacement rather than just cosmetic paint unless boxes prove sound.
- **Aging appliances/layout:** separate cooktop and wall oven, refrigerator sitting outside the main cabinet run, and limited clear counter space make the kitchen feel inefficient by current standards.
- **Potential water-risk area:** inspect closely under the sink, along the dishwasher/sink-side cabinets, and at the floor around the sink for soft spots, staining, rot, or subfloor damage.
- **Flooring condition:** heavily worn and likely needs removal. The floor should be checked once exposed, especially where there is visible discoloration/finish loss.
- **Lighting/electrical likely need updating:** pendant fixtures are dated, and there appear to be relatively few convenient task-lighting options. A renovation should account for recessed/task lighting, under-cabinet lighting, and updated outlets/GFCI protection.
- **Open shelving/window wall:** this is a visual liability now, but could become a feature—new window treatment, drywall/trim repair, or a redesigned sink/window zone could improve it substantially.

**Positive renovation signals:**
- The room has a reasonably efficient **U-/L-shaped work zone** with the sink, cooking area, and refrigerator fairly close together.
- There is meaningful cabinet volume and enough floor area for a compact dining table or potentially a more useful island/peninsula, depending on adjacent-room dimensions.
- The cabinet wall may allow a cleaner modern plan: full-height pantry storage, a standard range, relocated refrigerator, and longer uninterrupted counters.

**Likely scope:** At minimum, new flooring, cabinets or cabinet rehabilitation, countertops, sink/faucet, appliances, lighting, paint, and backsplash. A prudent buyer should budget for hidden plumbing, electrical, subfloor, and wall repairs until inspections/open-up confirm otherwise.

photo_005.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see a **clean, functional but dated bathroom with a strong “cosmetic-update” opportunity** rather than an obvious full gut requirement.

**What stands out:**
- **Narrow/linear layout:** Tub/shower, toilet, and vanity are tightly arranged, so moving plumbing may not be worthwhile unless a larger reconfiguration is planned.
- **Dated shower enclosure:** The textured sliding glass doors and metal framing are a clear age marker. Replacing them with a cleaner frameless/semi-frameless panel or a new tub surround would modernize the room quickly.
- **Builder-grade vanity and top:** White cabinet is serviceable, but the beige integrated sink/counter, small knobs, and traditional faucet date it. A new vanity top, faucet, hardware, and possibly vanity would have high visual impact.
- **Old-school mirrored medicine cabinet/light bar:** The multi-bulb “Hollywood” fixture and large mirrored cabinet are prime upgrade targets. Better vanity lighting and a framed mirror or modern recessed cabinet would change the feel significantly.
- **Floor tile/grout:** Beige ceramic tile appears intact but reads dated; grout condition and soundness should be checked. New large-format porcelain or LVP-rated-for-bath use could refresh it, though floor height and toilet reset need consideration.
- **Window/privacy:** Good natural light is a plus, but the blind and window trim look dated. A moisture-resistant privacy treatment or frosted film may be preferable; verify the window is well sealed given its proximity to wet areas.
- **Ventilation:** There appears to be a ceiling exhaust grille. A renovator would test whether it actually vents outdoors and has adequate airflow—important before investing in finishes.
- **Potential hidden-risk areas:** Inspect tub surround, shower-door tracks, caulk, floor perimeter, vanity base, and around the window for moisture damage. Nothing obvious is visible in the photo, but these are the likely trouble spots.

**Best value scope:** retain the existing layout; update shower enclosure/surround, vanity/top/faucet, lighting/mirror, flooring, paint, and accessories. A full remodel would mainly be justified if inspections reveal water damage or the goal is to enlarge/improve the shower experience.

photo_029.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely view this as a **tear-down or major rehab outbuilding**, not a quick cosmetic project.

Key takeaways:

- **Severe deferred maintenance:** missing/removed door, damaged siding and trim, deteriorated window, and an uneven/damaged threshold/floor area.
- **Interior appears compromised:** visible debris, exposed framing, and what may be moisture-related deterioration or floor damage. Roof condition cannot be confirmed from this angle, but the structure’s overall condition warrants inspection.
- **Site cleanup required:** scattered debris, overgrowth, and likely disposal costs are immediate scope items.
- **Access / usability issues:** the existing slab or walkway is broken and the entrance is not secure.
- **Mature wooded setting:** attractive privacy, but trees close to the building can mean ongoing leaf/moisture exposure and potential limb/root concerns.
- **Fence and adjacent utilities/fixtures:** chain-link fencing and the visible metal posts/fixtures should be identified before demolition or regrading.

Bottom line: budget for **cleanup, demolition or structural repair, and possibly replacement** rather than assuming this shed can be refreshed cheaply.

So the first stage that went wrong is Terra, which returned verdict "unsupported" with the rationale that the siding and trim "do not show clear rot, warping, cracks, or missing sections" -- contradicted by the visible panel deformation, corrosion and displaced trim -- and that verdict alone drove reason_code verdict_unsupported and disposition excluded. This is not the post-Terra routing gap, because Terra did not support the condition; it rejected it. Confidence is medium rather than higher because the truth basis is a single collapsed v1 verdict never re-adjudicated, and the damage, while real, is moderate rather than dramatic, so a stricter reading of "rot, warping, cracks, or missing sections" on corrugated metal is at least arguable.

A renovator would likely notice:

- **Awkward bedroom geometry:** The room is long and narrow, with a projecting/curved soffit or bulkhead along the right side and a beam across the ceiling. It limits furniture placement and makes the space feel more like a converted or reconfigured area than a clean rectangular bedroom.
- **Potentially low/uneven ceiling conditions:** The ceiling drops and boxed-in areas deserve investigation—could simply conceal HVAC, plumbing, or structure, but should be understood before opening walls.
- **Odd door/transom setup:** The closet door with the large transom-like opening above it, plus the nearby open doorway, creates visual clutter. A remodel could simplify this with a full-height closet system, revised door placement, or more cohesive trim.
- **Limited usable wall space:** The windows, closet, hall opening, and unusual ceiling leave relatively little uninterrupted wall area. Built-ins or a more deliberate furniture layout may add value.
- **Dated finishes:** Carpet, basic trim, flush-panel closet door, and the ceiling light fixture are straightforward cosmetic upgrade opportunities.
- **Window/egress and privacy check:** The narrow side windows appear small; confirm bedroom egress, insulation, and privacy treatment if this is being marketed as a bedroom.
- **Possible layout opportunity:** If adjacent hall/closet space permits, there may be an opportunity to improve closet storage or create a more defined primary-suite feel—but the ceiling bulkheads may constrain major changes.

The biggest question is what is inside the soffits/ceiling drops; that determines whether this is mostly a cosmetic refresh or a more involved reconfiguration.

prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed by direct inspection. The billed claim is dated_interior_trim = "interior trim plain, thin, or builder-grade trim package" in bedroom_3. In photo_021 the visible trim is a clean white six-panel colonial door with plain painted casing and a narrow painted baseboard (largely occluded by the bed and nightstand); in photo_023 the window carries a fairly substantial molded white casing with a sill and apron, plus a clean painted baseboard, and the same six-panel door. Everything is freshly painted, undamaged, and consistent with the room's staged/refreshed presentation — nothing in either frame shows trim that is dated, damaged, or in need of a replacement trim package, which matches the human v1.1 adjudication (claim absent, work none, hard_false_billed).

The false meaning is already fully formed in the 2a prose, before any structuring. Photo_021's 2a prose lists trim under a "Dated finishes" heading and calls it a cosmetic upgrade opportunity ("Carpet, basic trim, flush-panel closet door, and the ceiling light fixture are straightforward cosmetic upgrade opportunities"); photo_023's 2a prose does the same under "Potentially dated finishes: Beige walls, carpet, basic trim, and the simple interior door are easy cosmetic upgrade candidates." What 2a did NOT contain is any observation of trim damage, wear, undersizing, or stylistic obsolescence — it supplies no basis for the upgrade framing it asserts; it simply files ordinary, clean painted trim into a dated-finishes bucket. Every later stage carried that unchanged rather than distorting it: 2b produced faithful bullets ("The trim is basic." / "The room has beige walls, carpet, basic trim, and a simple interior door.") joined exact, 2c kept both, 2d resolved both to dated_interior_trim via exact_kind — a correct catalog mapping of "basic trim" — the issues projected to one condition, and Terra supported it. Since the unsupported material claim originates in the VLM prose itself, 2a is the first stage that went wrong.

photo_025.jpg.p2a_prose:
To a renovator, this bathroom reads as **clean, functional, and already partly updated—but with easy value-add opportunities**:

- **Good starting point:** Neutral paint, newer-looking vanity top, large framed mirror, and a modern black faucet mean it is not a full gut job.
- **Vanity is the main style mismatch:** The gray raised-panel cabinet and mixed hardware feel transitional/dated next to the contemporary faucet. Painting, swapping hardware, or installing a cleaner-lined vanity would modernize it quickly.
- **Lighting could be upgraded:** The visible ceiling light is basic; adding a decorative vanity light above the mirror would improve both function and resale appeal.
- **Mirror is oversized but plain:** It works well proportionally, though a framed statement mirror or paired mirrors/lights could give the room more character.
- **Window/privacy and trim:** The blind and deep window trim are serviceable but could be refreshed with a more polished privacy shade or frosted treatment.
- **Potential layout constraint:** The vanity is tightly positioned near the door/wall, so any replacement should preserve clearance and door swing.
- **Finish consistency:** Black faucet/towel ring contrast with silver cabinet knobs and door hardware. A coordinated hardware package—black, brushed nickel, or brass—would make the room feel intentionally designed.
- **No obvious red flags visible:** There are no apparent signs of water damage, cracked finishes, or major deterioration in this photo, though plumbing, flooring edges, ventilation, and the area around the window should be checked in person.

Overall: a **high-impact cosmetic renovation candidate**, likely needing finishes and fixtures more than structural work.

A renovator would likely see a **full exterior rehab candidate**, with a few high-priority risk areas:

- **Roof condition:** The shingles look aged and uneven, with visible waviness/sagging around the porch-roof connection. Budget for a roof replacement and have framing/decking inspected for rot or structural movement.
- **Porch:** The large covered porch is a strong resale feature, but its posts, fascia, railings, steps, and porch roof appear weathered. It may need substantial carpentry work—not just paint.
- **Wood siding/trim:** Extensive peeling paint and weathered wood suggest deferred maintenance. Expect scraping, repairs/replacement of deteriorated boards, and a full paint system. Check carefully for hidden rot and possible pest damage.
- **Foundation / low crawlspace concerns:** The house sits fairly low, and some porch supports/foundation areas look worn. A renovator should inspect for settling, moisture, inadequate ventilation, and joist/sill deterioration.
- **Windows and openings:** Older mismatched-looking windows and worn trim could mean poor efficiency and possible water intrusion. Replacement or restoration should be in the scope.
- **Drainage and site:** The flat yard and limited apparent drainage detail raise moisture-management concerns. Gutters, downspouts, grading, and drainage should be evaluated early.
- **Cosmetic upside:** The basic form, large front porch, mature trees, and apparent street presence give it character. If the structure is sound, exterior restoration could create a dramatic before-and-after.

Biggest unknowns from this photo: **roof framing, foundation/crawlspace condition, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and whether exterior deterioration is superficial or reflects widespread rot.** A contractor walk-through and structural/pest inspection would be essential before pricing the project.

prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed by inspection: photo_001.jpg shows a full-width covered porch whose roof fascia/soffit line is visibly wavy rather than straight, with a dark ragged band of out-of-plane, deteriorated boards where the porch roof meets the main house above the steps. That is consistent with the adjudicated v1.1 axes (claim=exact, work=warranted), so the condition is real and the pipeline failed to bill it.

The 2a prose DID contain the condition, in plain terms: under "Roof condition" it states the shingles look aged and uneven "with visible waviness/sagging around the porch-roof connection," and separately notes the porch's "fascia, railings, steps, and porch roof appear weathered" and "may need substantial carpentry work-not just paint." What the 2a prose did NOT contain is the specific vocabulary of the catalog item ("soffit," "porch ceiling panels," "loose or missing panels") -- it described the same physical defect at the porch-roof connection in roof/framing language rather than soffit language. That wording gap did not cost anything downstream: 2b lifted the sentence verbatim as bullet index 1 (exact join), 2c kept it (p2c_present true, and the only 2c drops on this photo are four benign non-defect bullets: low house, flat yard, large porch, mature trees), 2d resolved it via the llm path to soffit_or_porch_ceiling_failed on exact_kind routing -- a resolution the human's "exact" claim axis explicitly ratifies, so 2d is not the fault -- 2e kept the issue (p2e_status kept, issue id present in kept_issue_ids), and condition_projection produced oc1_69263601050587ce.

So the condition survived intact all the way to the final verdict, and the first and only stage that went wrong is terra: it returned cannot_assess with the rationale that "the porch ceiling or soffit panels are not clearly visible enough to judge sagging, looseness, or missing panels," which set accepted=false with reason_code verdict_cannot_assess. Terra's non-assessment is what dropped a claim the human found exactly supported and warranted, on a photo where the sagging porch-roof/soffit line is in fact discernible. This is NOT the known post-Terra routing gap: that gap applies only when Terra SUPPORTED the condition and disposition still unbilled it. Here Terra did not support it -- cannot_assess is itself the terminal non-accept -- so the ladder has a rung that fits, and the "inspection" disposition is a consequence of Terra's verdict rather than an independent routing decision. The 2e note in the record (one tier_optional_suppressed count on this photo) is a red herring per the stated corpus rule and, in any case, this issue was kept and projected.

photo_017.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see this as a **full-gut bathroom**, not a cosmetic refresh.

- **Clear moisture/water damage:** Deteriorated wall material around and beneath the sink/toilet, staining at the shower curb and floor, and possible mold or rot indications. The source and extent need investigation before finishes go in.
- **Plumbing concerns:** Exposed, aged drain/supply lines under the sink; the shower valve/trim appears incomplete or damaged. Budget for updating supply, drains, shutoffs, and potentially venting.
- **Shower needs rebuilding:** The shower looks unfinished or heavily compromised, with a questionable curb/pan condition and old wall tile. Assume demolition to framing/subfloor and a new properly waterproofed pan and surround.
- **Old finishes throughout:** Dated tile, damaged flooring, worn fixtures, old medicine cabinet, mirror/light area, and likely several layers of prior patchwork.
- **Electrical/ventilation should be checked:** The fixture area looks outdated, and there is no obvious exhaust fan. A remodel should include GFCI-protected outlets, modern lighting, and venting to the exterior.
- **Potential hidden structural/subfloor work:** The staining and deterioration at the floor-wall junction make subfloor, framing, and toilet flange condition important inspection items.

The upside is that it appears to be a compact, straightforward layout with the core fixtures already grouped together, so keeping the general footprint could control costs. But I’d price it as demolition, remediation, plumbing/electrical review, waterproofing, and complete replacement—not simply new tile and paint.

A renovator would likely see a **full gut-or-major-refresh kitchen**, but also a workable footprint and plenty of upside.

**What stands out immediately:**
- **Very dated finishes:** raised-panel cabinets, laminate/parquet-style flooring, tile backsplash, soffit/upper cabinetry, old lighting, and the built-in wall oven/cooktop arrangement all read several decades old.

- **Open shelving/window wall:** this is a visual liability now, but could become a feature—new window treatment, drywall/trim repair, or a redesigned sink/window zone could improve it substantially.

**Positive renovation signals:**
- The room has a reasonably efficient **U-/L-shaped work zone** with the sink, cooking area, and refrigerator fairly close together.
- There is meaningful cabinet volume and enough floor area for a compact dining table or potentially a more useful island/peninsula, depending on adjacent-room dimensions.
